section.title: Installing
section.para: You need ooRexx 5.3.0 r13329 or later (a beta, from SourceForge), Python 3.9 or later, and the bridge, from the project's releases page, https://github.com/JosepMariaBlasco/oorexxpython/releases.

On Windows, download oorexxpython-version-windows-x64.exe and run it. It finds ooRexx and the Pythons installed on the computer (from python.org or the Microsoft Store), and asks which of them will import the bridge and which one Rexx programs use. It also puts these books and the samples' slide deck in ooRexx's Start menu folder, and can be uninstalled from Settings > Apps.

On Linux and macOS, download the zip for your system, unzip it, open a terminal in the unzipped folder, and run its installer (the zip works on Windows too: rexx install, from a terminal opened as administrator):

Either way, the bridge goes into your ooRexx, becomes importable from your Python, and both directions are checked: the installation ends with ooRexx/Python: installed and OK. The samples are then in ooRexx's samples folder, under python. The project's README.md has the details for each system.

One bridge works with every Python from 3.9 on: it uses only Python's Stable ABI. A Rexx program uses the Python named by the environment variable ORX_PYTHON, or else the one chosen when the bridge was installed, or else the python3 on the PATH (python on Windows), with its installed packages: install numpy, matplotlib and pandas there (pip install numpy matplotlib pandas) for the samples that use them.

section.title: Calling Python from Rexx
section.para: You want to use a Python module from a Rexx program.

How it works. ::requires "python.cls" loads the bridge and Python with it, and defines .py, the way in: it is Python's builtins plus a few helpers, import first among them. .py~import("math") returns the module, and its functions are called as Rexx messages: math~sqrt(2) is math.sqrt(2). A function without arguments is called too, so math~pi is the constant, and math~factorial(30) a function call.
Python's numbers come back as Rexx strings, with all their digits: Python's integers have no size limit, and the result of factorial is exact, whatever Rexx's NUMERIC DIGITS.
See also Reference, Introduction and Python Class.

section.title: Calling Rexx from Python
section.para: You want to run Rexx code from a Python program.

How it works. import oorexx is the bridge, seen from Python. oorexx.Interpreter() creates an ooRexx interpreter instance; as a context manager it is closed at the end of the with block. eval evaluates an expression, routine makes a routine from source, callable as a Python function, and run calls a program file with arguments.

Rexx's results come to Python by the same rule as Python's come to Rexx (): a Rexx string that is a number comes as an int or a float. 2 ** 100 with Rexx's default nine digits is 1.26765060E+30, a float; with forty digits it is exact, an int. What the Rexx code says goes through Python's sys.stdout, marked REXXout> ().

section.title: Running the Samples
section.para: Each recipe says how to run its sample: rexx 01-hello.rex in the folder where the samples are, or python3 30-run-rexx.py (python on Windows). The bridge's installer copies them into ooRexx's samples folder, under python.
When the bridge is built from source instead of installed, the repository's samples/run-one.sh runs a sample with the build: samples/run-one.sh 01-hello.rex 3.11 runs it with Python 3.11.
